subject: Anthropology
title: The Gift
description: A quick, practical guide to The Gift.

hook.text: Marcel Mauss asked a simple question: if a gift is free, why do we feel obligated to give one back?

buildup.text: Mauss studied gift exchange and found three obligations: to give, to receive, and to reciprocate.

discovery.text: Gifts create social bonds. Refusing a gift is an insult; failing to reciprocate breaks the relationship.

twist.text: The gift is never free. It carries the giver's spirit and creates a debt that ties people together.

climax.text: Gift exchange is the original economy — not about profit, but about building and maintaining social ties.

punchline.text: Every gift is a bond disguised as generosity.

quiz.question: What did Mauss discover about gift exchange?
options: Gifts create obligations to give, receive, and reciprocate

details.summary: Marcel Mauss's The Gift (1925) argued that gift-giving is never truly free — gifts create obligations to receive and reciprocate, binding people in webs of social debt. This analysis revealed that exchange systems structure social relationships far more deeply than economics recognized.
details.whyItMatters: Mauss showed that economies are always social systems, not just material transactions. Gift exchange creates and maintains relationships, making it the foundation of social life in many societies and still active in our own.
takeaways: Mauss argued gifts create obligations to receive and reciprocate
Gift exchange binds people in webs of social debt and connection
Economies are social systems, not just material transactions

faq.question: What are the three obligations of gift exchange according to Mauss?
faq.answer: The obligation to give, the obligation to receive, and the obligation to reciprocate. Refusing a gift insults the giver. Failing to reciprocate creates unresolvable social debt. These obligations bind people together in ongoing relationships of mutual dependence.

faq.question: Does gift exchange still matter in modern market economies?
faq.answer: Absolutely. Birthday presents, business gifts, dinner invitations, and holiday exchanges all follow Mauss's logic. The social obligations attached to gifts structure relationships in boardrooms and families just as they do in Melanesian exchange systems.
